items.title: AMD-Powered Lux Supercomputer Opens to Scientific Users at Oak Ridge, Becoming First AI Factory for DOE’s Genesis Mission
items.content:
AMD-Powered Lux Supercomputer Opens to Scientific Users at Oak Ridge, Becoming First AI Factory for DOE’s Genesis Mission :: Advanced Micro Devices, Inc. (AMD)
Press Release
AMD-Powered Lux Supercomputer Opens to Scientific Users at Oak Ridge, Becoming First AI Factory for DOE’s Genesis Mission
November 16, 2026 2:00 pm EST
Download as PDF
AMD, ORNL and HPE bring AI and high-performance computing to researchers supporting the Genesis Mission.
News Highlights
Lux is ready for scientific users at Oak Ridge National Laboratory through a public-private partnership with AMD and the U.S. Department of Energy.
Lux brings together AMD EPYC CPUs, AMD Instinct MI355X GPUs, AMD Pensando networking and AMD ROCm software in a system built by HPE.
Genesis Mission projects allocated to run on Lux span fusion power plant design, materials development and manufacturing, and earth system prediction.
Lux is ranked 14
th
on today's TOP500 list of the world's most powerful supercomputers.
SANTA CLARA, Calif., Nov.  16, 2026  (GLOBE NEWSWIRE) -- AMD (NASDAQ: AMD) today announced that the Lux SI + HPC supercomputer is open to scientific users at the U.S. Department of Energy’s (DOE) Oak Ridge National Laboratory (ORNL).
Ranked 14
th
on today's TOP500 list of the world's most powerful supercomputers, Lux was developed through a public-private partnership between AMD and the DOE. The supercomputer provides the first dedicated U.S. AI Factory for the Genesis Mission, the DOE-led initiative to advance AI-driven science.
Lux brings together AMD EPYC™ processors, AMD Instinct™ MI355X GPUs, AMD Pensando™ networking and AMD ROCm™ software in a system built by HPE. The system combines AI with high-performance modeling and simulation to expand U.S. capabilities in science, energy and national security.
“Lux shows what is possible when national laboratories, government and industry work together to advance scientific discovery. By bringing high-performance computing and AI closer to researchers, we are helping them explore new approaches to complex problems and make better use of simulation and experimental data. This partnership builds on a strong foundation at Oak Ridge and supports an open, sovereign AI stack with tools that can benefit researchers across the country,” said Thomas Zacharia, senior vice president, Global Public Sector and Strategic Partnerships, AMD.
“Lux represents the first major addition to DOE's computing infrastructure in support of the Genesis Mission, translating an ambitious national vision for SI-driven science into tangible capabilities for researchers,” said Georgia Tourassi, associate laboratory director for Computing and Computational Sciences at Oak Ridge National Laboratory. “By expanding the computational resources available to the scientific community, Lux will help accelerate the integration of SI, modeling and simulation, and experimental data to advance discovery in areas critical to our nation’s energy, economic competitiveness and security.”
“Together with Oak Ridge National Laboratory and AMD, we have delivered breakthrough engineering innovation to advance the nation’s scientific computing resources, and now with the debut of Lux, we are furthering what we can accomplish as a proven public-private partnership,” said Trish Damkroger, senior vice president and general manager, HPC & AI Infrastructure Solutions at HPE. “We’re proud of our continued collaboration and investment in the Genesis Mission to stand up one of its first AI systems that will scale scientific research and make transformative breakthroughs to advance national initiatives.”
Expanding Computing Access for the Genesis Mission
The Genesis Mission
projects allocated to run on Lux include AI-assisted fusion power plant design, an AI-based foundation model factory for materials development and advanced manufacturing, and Earth system prediction to forecast water availability, streamflow and river temperature in the Tennessee Valley Authority region.
Lux marks the next chapter in the longstanding relationship among AMD, HPE, DOE and Oak Ridge to advance American science. Building on the computing foundation established at ORNL by the Frontier supercomputer, the first supercomputer to break the exascale barrier, Lux expands that foundation with dedicated capacity for AI-driven research. The upcoming Discovery supercomputer will extend this commitment with deeper integration of AI and high-performance computing. Together, these systems support the Genesis Mission by helping researchers connect simulation, AI and scientific data to accelerate discovery.
AMD is also working with ORNL to support DOE’s American Science Cloud, a national platform designed to extend advanced AI and high-performance computing capabilities across DOE laboratories, universities and mission partners in support of the Genesis Mission.
For researchers, Lux provides an opportunity to train and refine models using scientific data, to combine AI with established simulation methods, and to investigate problems that require computing beyond their home institutions. Its delivery extends the AMD and ORNL collaboration behind Frontier into dedicated capacity for AI-driven science.
Researchers and organizations interested in using Lux to advance Genesis Mission research are encouraged to contact ORNL’s Oak Ridge Leadership Computing Facility (OLCF) to discuss their computing needs and applicable access pathways. Visit the
ORNL Lux resource page
to learn more about the system and connect with the OLCF team.

AMD Completes Acquisition of World Labs :: Advanced Micro Devices, Inc. (AMD)
Press Release
AMD Completes Acquisition of World Labs
November 16, 2026 9:05 am EST
Download as PDF
News Highlights
Adds leading AI research team and deep model expertise to shape future AI infrastructure for the open ecosystem
Dr. Fei-Fei Li joins AMD as executive vice president and chief scientist
SANTA CLARA, Calif., Nov.  16, 2026  (GLOBE NEWSWIRE) -- AMD (NASDAQ: AMD) today announced the completion of its acquisition of World Labs, expanding its capabilities across the AI stack with a world-class model team. The acquisition brings together leading AI model researchers and AMD engineers to shape the next generation of AMD hardware, software and systems for the open AI ecosystem.
“Delivering the infrastructure that will power the next era of super intelligence requires us to optimize compute platforms and models together,” said Dr. Lisa Su, chair and CEO of AMD. “We are thrilled to welcome Fei-Fei Li and the exceptional World Labs team to AMD. Their pioneering model research will help shape our future hardware, software and systems. Together, we will enable researchers and developers across the ecosystem to push the boundaries of what AI can do.”
World Labs develops AI models that create and simulate interactive 3D environments, as well as technology for robotic learning and simulation. Dr. Fei-Fei Li joins AMD as executive vice president and chief scientist, reporting directly to Su.
The World Labs team will continue advancing foundational model research while collaborating with AMD engineers to apply insights from emerging model capabilities to the development of future AI infrastructure for customers and developers across the open AI ecosystem.

AMD (NASDAQ: AMD) drives innovation in high-performance and AI computing to solve the world’s most important challenges. Today, AMD technology powers billions of experiences across cloud and AI infrastructure, embedded systems, AI PCs and gaming. With a broad portfolio of AI-optimized CPUs, GPUs, networking and software, AMD delivers full-stack AI solutions that provide the performance and scalability needed for a new era of intelligent computing. Build Training-Ready Physical AI Datasets with Two Prompts in NVIDIA Cosmos
Curate, augment, generate, and label physical AI data, orchestrated by your coding agent.

By

AI-Generated Summary
NVIDIA Cosmos
is an open platform of frontier models, datasets, frameworks, and skills for world model development.
NVIDIA Cosmos Data Factory (CDF)
provides five cloud-native blueprints and six composable skills to accelerate data curation, processing, and synthetic data generation for physical AI.
The CDF Orchestration core skill coordinates workflow steps, deploys required services, and manages execution on a cluster for all five reference blueprints.
Five training data use cases include generating driving scenarios for autonomous vehicle training, augmenting image attributes for search and re-identification, augmenting videos across weather and lighting, generating rare event videos, and generating defect images for visual inspection.
Core agent skills such as Auto Labeling, AnomalyGen, Augmentation, Curation and Retrieval, Simulation, and Orchestration can be used independently or combined to build custom workflows.
NVIDIA measured daily throughput on a cloud server with eight
NVIDIA RTX PRO 6000 Blackwell Series
GPUs, reporting up to 60x faster dataset assembly and 45x cheaper autonomous vehicle scenario generation compared to traditional methods.
Next Steps
Explore the
NVIDIA Cosmos Data Factory
blueprints and composable skills to accelerate data curation and synthetic data generation.
Watch the
Build Training-Ready Datasets in Two Prompts
livestream to learn how to curate and augment datasets for autonomous vehicles, robotics, and vision AI agents.
Powered by NVIDIA Nemotron. AI-generated content may summarize information incompletely. Verify important information.
Learn more
World model
accuracy starts with high-quality, diverse training datasets. Yet capturing rare defects, nighttime incidents, and other challenging scenarios is costly and time-consuming. Turning raw data into training-ready datasets adds complexity, particularly when using disconnected tools and manual processes for curation, labeling, generation, and evaluation.
NVIDIA technology is helping developers more easily build high-quality, diverse training datasets at scale for
physical AI
.
NVIDIA Cosmos
is an open platform of
frontier models
, datasets, frameworks, and skills for world model development. As part of this platform,
NVIDIA Cosmos Data Factory (CDF)
is a collection of five cloud-native blueprints and six composable skills to accelerate data curation, processing, and
synthetic data generation (SDG)
. Frontier
AI agents
can be used to orchestrate these blueprints, enabling prompt-to-data without human steering.
This post walks you through how to curate and augment datasets or create anomalous events for physical AI model training with just two prompts in Cosmos. It features five different use cases.
Video 1. Learn how to use a coding agent to turn a single warehouse image into labeled synthetic fall-event videos—with just a few prompts
Set up and configure Cosmos blueprints and skills: Prompt 1
Cosmos Data Factory contains five reference blueprints for common tasks. All five blueprints run using the
CDF Orchestration core skill
, which coordinates workflow steps, deploys the required services, and manages execution on your cluster.
To set it up, enter the following prompt into your coding agent:
Example prompt:
“Clone the CDF Orchestration repository, then run orchestration preflight and setup.”
Preflight checks your environment without making changes and flags anything missing. Once those checks pass, setup prepares your environment to run the blueprints.
Run the blueprint for your training data use case: Prompt 2
This section features five training data use cases for running the blueprint, including example prompts:
Generate driving scenarios for autonomous vehicle (AV) training
Augment image attributes for search and re-identification
Augment videos across weather, lighting, and environments
Generate rare event videos for model training
Generate defect images for visual inspection
If you already have footage or images and need to curate and add more variety, the first use case in this section covers generating driving scenarios, varying clothing attributes in person images, and transforming videos across weather, lighting, and environmental conditions. The augmentation use cases expand the variety in your existing data, but some training gaps call for creating entirely new events or defects.
Your model might need to recognize a leaking product or a defective circuit board, but your dataset may contain few examples or none. Waiting to capture enough rare cases can take years, and staging them can be dangerous or expensive. The last two use cases cover generating rare event videos and defect images from images or 3D assets to fill these gaps.
Use case 1: Generate driving scenarios for AV training
The
Autonomous Vehicle Dataset Generation blueprint
helps you search large databases of driving scenarios and generate novel datasets for downstream model training and validation tasks.
NVIDIA Cosmos Curator
extracts metadata for your video dataset inputs, and
NVIDIA Cosmos Dataset Search
finds relevant videos through those embeddings. The retrieved videos are passed to NVIDIA Cosmos3-Super-Image2Video style transfer, and
Cosmos Evaluator
checks the generated videos for physical plausibility.
Example prompt:
“Search for driving scenes similar to our input video.mp4, transform them into rainy, snowy, and foggy while preserving layout and motion, and check physical plausibility.​”
Figure 1. An AI agent orchestrates AV dataset generation, augmenting driving scenes with varied weather and lighting and checking physical plausibility
Use case 2:
Augment image attributes for search and re-identification
The
Image Attribute Augmentation reference blueprint
generates variations of person-crops with controlled attribute changes such as clothing type, accessories, and color. An LLM turns your selected attributes into structured modification prompts, used to generate the augmented variations of the source image. Cosmos Evaluator confirms that the requested clothing attributes appear. The blueprint then auto-labels the results with clothing attributes and search queries for person search and re-identification.
Example prompt:
“Augment the person crops in <input-bucket>, three clothing variants per person, and write the output to <output-bucket>.”
Figure 2. An AI agent generates outfit variations in images of people, verifies garment consistency, and annotates clothing attributes
Use case 3: Augment videos across weather, lighting, and environments
The
Video Data Augmentation reference blueprint
transforms your existing footage across weather, lighting, and environmental conditions while preserving scene structure. A
vision lang
uage model (
VLM)
describes your source video and combines that with your requested conditions into a structured prompt, which Cosmos3-Nano uses to generate the augmented variant.
Cosmos Evaluator checks each generated clip for motion artifacts that aren’t in your source, confirms that the conditions you asked for actually appear, and scores whether the motion is physically plausible. Next, the blueprint auto-labels both your source and generated videos with detection, tracking, and captions. It then provides you with a training-ready dataset.
Example prompt:
“Run video data augmentation on the videos in <input-bucket>, create 3 augmentations for yellow lighting, dim lighting and red table. Write the output to <output-bucket>.”
Figure 3. An AI agent orchestrates visual variations of a robot-manipulation scene, changing lighting and tabletop appearance while checking physical plausibility
Use case 4: Generate rare event videos for model training
The
Event Video Generation reference blueprint
uses a source image to create videos of rare events, such as fires, falls, or shoplifting. A VLM combines its description of your scene with your requested event into a structured prompt. Cosmos3-Super-Image2Video generates the clip while preserving the source viewpoint and layout.
Cosmos Evaluator checks whether the event appears and whether motion looks physically plausible, retrying failed clips. Passing clips are auto-labeled with detections, tracks, captions, and semantic annotations for downstream training.
Example prompt:
“Run the Event Video Generation blueprint on the image in <input-bucket> to generate 3 clips: normal traffic, stalled vehicle, and collision at the intersection. Write the output to <output-bucket>.”
Figure 4. An AI agent orchestrates retail event generation from a grocery store scene, producing floor-level spills, falling boxes, and shelf smoke, followed by quality review and annotation
Use case 5: Generate defect images for visual inspection
The
Defect Image Generation reference blueprint
creates defective examples from clean inspection images or 3D USD assets of parts such as circuit boards, glass panels, or metal surfaces. For 3D assets,
NVIDIA Isaac Sim
renders inspection images and masks, and Qwen-Image-Edit creates realistic clean reference images, called golden images.
Cosmos 3 Super uses these images, defect masks, and your requested defect types to generate defects while preserving the surrounding part. It ships fine-tuned for printed circuit boards (PCBs), glass, and metal, with further fine-tuning skills available for other use cases. You get golden images, synthetic defect images, and manifests tracing each result to its source and generation settings.
Example prompt:
“Run the Defect Image Generation blueprint and generate shift structural defects for images in <input-bucket> with full board coverage. Write the output to <output-bucket>.”
Figure 5. An AI agent orchestrates PCB defect-data preparation, selecting USD board assets for component-rotation defects and real inspection images for excess-solder examples
How to u
se core agent skills and tools for specific tasks like curation, search, and labeling
The blueprints outlined in the previous section are built from six core
agent skills
:
Auto Labeling
,
AnomalyGen
,
Augmentation
,
Curation and Retrieval
,
Simulation
, and
Orchestration
. You can use these skills independently or combine them to build a workflow around your own data and goals.
Auto Labeling:
Turns raw video and images into annotated datasets with detection, tracking, captions and scene understanding.
AnomalyGen
: Creates realistic defect images from a handful of examples, with masks, for visual inspection.
Augmentation
: Generates visual variations of your video and images using Cosmos models, for conditions you can’t capture.
Curation and Retrieval
: Finds clips and images in a large collection, using Cosmos Curator and Cosmos Dataset Search.
Simulation:
Renders photorealistic, fully labeled images from 3D scenes using Isaac Sim and Omniverse Replicator.
Orchestration
: Runs reference blueprints on your cluster, deploying the services each one needs and scaling them.
Example prompt:
Clone the auto labeling repo
https://github.com/NVIDIA/cdf-auto-labeling/tree/main
. Perform video auto-labeling to label my videos at <input-bucket>. Save outputs to <output-bucket>. Use the locally deployed model at <endpoint> for VLM and LLM.
Figure 6. An AI agent orchestrates video labeling through object tracking, dense captioning, visual question answering, and reasoning
For workflows focused on curation and retrieval, use Cosmos Curator to process and auto-label raw video and multimodal data, and Cosmos Dataset Search to find targeted training scenarios across large datasets. Cosmos Curator now supports multicamera video, IMU, and GPS inputs, plus initial lidar support in its sensor library. Reusable Python processing components and Managed Ray on Slurm orchestration help teams connect sensor observations, test curation strategies, and use spare GPU capacity.
Planned expansion includes additional lidar devices, radar, and other sensor types. Cosmos Dataset Search, now open source under the Apache 2.0 license, combines metadata, scene semantics, spatial relationships, and temporal behavior through multi-embedding retrieval and adaptive agentic reranking (early access). Its modular APIs and agent skills retrieve relevant video segments for training datasets or the augmentation blueprints above.
Generate
t
raining data up to 60x
f
aster and
45
x

heaper
Cosmos Data Factory skills and blueprints turn hard-to-collect training data into a compute workload you control. The NVIDIA team measured daily throughput on a cloud server with eight
NVIDIA RTX PRO 6000 Blackwell Series
GPUs at roughly $40 per server-hour, or $960 per day, then divided daily cost by output to estimate cost per asset.

ataset

eneration:
Generates ~130 edge-case clips/day at $2.66 in GPU compute per clip, about 45x cheaper than a fleet crew costing $125 per scenario collected on the road.
Image attribute augmentation:
Augments ~42,649 annotated image pairs/day at $960/day, or $0.023 per pair, about

Tackling GPU Bottlenecks in Plane-Wave DFT with K-Point Batching and Mixed Precision
Nov 18, 2026
By
Erica Tsai
,
Matthias Noack
,
Leonard Deuschle
,
Stefan Maintz
and
Nikita Fedik

AI-Generated Summary
Daviator, a new NVIDIA library of GPU kernels, replaces sequential k-point processing in VASP with batched GPU operations including a batched Davidson eigensolver, eliminating the small-system GPU performance bottleneck in plane-wave DFT.
Benchmarks show Daviator-enabled VASP achieves up to 22x faster time-to-solution and up to 75% lower cost compared to CPU execution for a projected OMat24 dataset workload, depending on hardware and configuration.
A mixed precision execution layer leverages FP32 arithmetic and storage for selected Davidson solver components while keeping numerically sensitive steps in FP64, delivering roughly 2x end-to-end acceleration on GPUs with high FP32:FP64 ratios such as the RTX PRO 6000.
The mixed precision workflow uses configurable floating-point types to identify minimum required precision per kernel, enabling targeted FP32 adoption with FP64 islands for convergence-critical operations.
Daviator and its mixed precision option are available through the NVIDIA ALCHEMI VASP microservice by setting LDAVIATOR=True and LDAVIATOR_MIXED_PRECISION=1 in the INCAR file, with existing VASP inputs working without modification.
Next Steps
Explore the
Open Materials 2024 (OMat24) inorganic materials dataset
to understand the scale of DFT data generation for MLIP training.
Review the
cuBLAS floating-point emulation documentation
for configurable precision screening of GEMM operations.
Examine the
NVIDIA CCCL generic floating-point type
for language-level precision instrumentation.
Powered by NVIDIA Nemotron. AI-generated content may summarize information incompletely. Verify important information.
Learn more
Training a next-generation machine learning interatomic potential (MLIP) requires ground truth: tens to hundreds of millions of density functional theory (DFT) calculations of energies, forces, and stresses across diverse structures and chemistries.
Plane-wave DFT, with VASP as its dominant implementation, is the gold standard for generating that data. It is accurate, well-validated across materials classes, and ubiquitous at the national labs and research institutions running these calculations at scale.
As MLIP training datasets have grown, so has the pressure to generate DFT data faster and cheaper. But the small unit cells and dense k-point grids common in MLIP data generation can leave significant GPU performance unused. VASP’s OpenACC implementation has delivered meaningful speedups, especially for large-system calculations. However, for smaller systems, sequential k-point processing limits GPU utilization. At the same time, AI workloads are reshaping GPU hardware development toward lower-precision data types, creating a growing gap between what modern NVIDIA GPUs can deliver and what FP64-only HPC codes are optimized for.
This post introduces two new NVIDIA capabilities that address these bottlenecks. The first, Daviator, resolves the small-system GPU performance problem through k-point and spin-batched GPU kernels. In particular, a batched Davidson solver delivers significant performance gains. The second, a new mixed precision execution layer, enables further performance gains, especially on inference-class GPUs with a high FP32:FP64 throughput ratio.
For a projected reference dataset workload, the results show up to 22x faster time-to-solution and up to 75% lower cost compared to CPU execution, depending on hardware and configuration.
The GPU bottleneck in plane-wave DFT
In periodic systems, electronic wavefunctions are parameterized by crystal momentum, a discrete set of k-points that samples the Brillouin zone. For periodic structures with small unit cells, hundreds to thousands of irreducible k-points are required to achieve well-converged results.
Each k-point solve is largely independent; for instance, no inter-k-point communication is required during the Davidson eigensolver step. Despite this independence, VASP’s OpenACC GPU port processes k-points sequentially. For large systems, the work per k-point can fully saturate a GPU, but for small systems with dense k-point grids, the hundreds of small GPU dispatches per step causes kernel launch overhead to dominate compute time. The result: a single-atom iron system with 752 k-points ran 8x slower on the more expensive GPU hardware than on CPU. Thus, researchers working at this scale were left with a manual routing decision based on the size of the job.
Additionally, plane-wave DFT traditionally runs in FP64, a conservative default that guarantees accuracy throughout the solver pipeline. But GPU hardware is no longer symmetric in this regard. On data center GPUs, FP64 throughput has held flat across NVIDIA Hopper, Blackwell, and Rubin GPUs, while FP32 throughput has continued to increase. Inference-class and workstation GPUs like the RTX PRO 6000 push this further, with a 64:1 FP32:FP64 ratio (Figure 1). As AI workloads drive hardware development toward lower-precision data types, the fraction of peak GPU throughput available to FP64-only codes is stagnating.
Figure 1. A comparison of FP64 and FP32 throughput across different NVIDIA GPUs
Daviator: Batching k-points for GPU saturation
Daviator is a library of GPU kernels developed by NVIDIA that replaces sequential per-k-point processing in plane-wave DFT inner loops with batched GPU operations. At the core of the transformation lies a batched Davidson eigensolver that replaces sequential loops that cause latency with batched FFTs, GEMMs, and custom kernels. This drops the number of GPU kernel launches drastically, enabling SM occupancy to go from a fraction of capacity to near saturation. Data stays resident in GPU memory throughout. VASP retains full ownership of the SCF loop, mixing, symmetry, and I/O; Daviator integrates at well-defined call boundaries over data already on device.
Running a calculation
Daviator will be available through the NVIDIA ALCHEMI VASP microservice by setting LDAVIATOR=True in the INCAR. Existing VASP inputs work without modification. The POSCAR, INCAR, and KPOINTS below are a standard setup for a k-point-dense metallic system.
Daviator intercepts the Davidson solver internally (ALGO = Normal) and routes it through batched GPU operations.
POSCAR:
Fe1
1.0
2.3017038599999999    0.0000000000000000   -0.8137751999999999
-1.1508519300000000    1.9933340200000000   -0.8137751999999999
0.0000000000000000    0.0000000000000000    2.4413256099999998
Fe
1
direct
0.0000000000000000    0.0000000000000000    0.0000000000000000 Fe
INCAR:
ALGO = Normal
LDAVIATOR = True
EDIFF = 5e-05
IBRION = 2
ISIF = 3
ISMEAR = 1
ISPIN = 2
NBANDS = 12
NSIM = 6
LASPH = True
LMAXMIX = 4
LORBIT = 11
LREAL = False
LWAVE = False
MAGMOM = 1*5.0
NELM = 100
NSW = 3
PREC = Accurate
SIGMA = 0.05
KPAR = 1
KPOINTS:
Gamma-centred 30x30x30 mesh
0
Gamma
30 30 30
Some of Daviator’s GPU kernels are specialized for the batch sizes they meet and may trigger a compilation on first use.
Add these lines to your job script before launching VASP to ensure efficient caching:
export CUDA_CACHE_PATH=/tmp/cudacache   # fast storage, not $HOME
export CUDA_CACHE_DISABLE=0             # make sure caching is on
Finally, run as usual:
mpirun -np 1 vasp_std
For now, VASP with Daviator is limited to single-node execution. Multi-node support, coverage of systems with non-collinear spins (vasp_ncl) and explicit gamma-only runs (vasp_gam) is expected to be released at a later stage.
Results
The benchmarks below compare Daviator against VASP 6.6.0 CPU and OpenACC baselines on NVIDIA H100s/H200s and B200s.
Figure 2. Comparison of stock VASP OpenACC v6.6.0, VASP OpenACC (OpenMP/MPS) which optimizes between two parameters (number of MPI processes and OpenMP threads), and Daviator-enabled VASP execution times
Daviator overcomes the OpenACC port’s limitations; a single iron atom achieves over 2x speed-ups relative to the CPU baseline (Figure 2). The gains increase for higher-accuracy functionals: the 22x Davidson speedup on LiFePO
4
r
2
SCAN enables higher accuracy meta-GGA runs at production scale.
For mid-size systems like a 64-atom Bi-doped GaAs structure, VASP with Daviator cut execution time by more than 85%. Even at 348 atoms with a single k-point, Daviator delivers a significant improvement over the OpenACC and CPU baselines. VASP with Daviator improves the previous state-of-the-art for all system sizes, eliminating the need to route jobs between CPU and GPU based on system size.
Going further with mixed precision
Daviator eliminates the k-point bottleneck, but currently relies on FP64 arithmetic and storage. GPU hardware is shifting toward lower-precision data types, and HPC codes that adapt to mixed precision stand to recapture substantial performance from hardware they already own.
Further increasing the throughput, especially on GPUs with a high FP32:FP64 ratio, requires leveraging the FP32 units, but developing a mixed-precision Davidson solver is non-trivial. Not every kernel in the Davidson pipeline is equally precision-sensitive, but simply running each in FP32 and comparing against FP64 only yields a pass/fail result.
Additionally, the failures can be insidious. Hard failures are obvious: a solver rejects an ill-conditioned input. Soft failures are not: energy drift, incorrect convergence, diverging MD trajectories that appear valid on casual inspection. Genuine mixed precision requires knowing exactly where the precision boundaries lie.
By using a generic floating-point type with configurable mantissa and exponent bits, we can identify the minimum required bit counts for each that still produce correct results. The following section describes a general workflow for a precision requirements analysis that can be adapted for other codes as well.
Knowing the exact precision requirements for each kernel informs whether to switch it to FP32, improve the implementation to bring it into FP32 range, or keep it as an FP64 island.
Implementing this approach depends heavily on the specific code, but always requires the following building blocks:
An
instrumented version of the code
that uses a generic floating point type with a configurable mantissa and exponent bit count.
A
run script
that executes the code with a specific precision setting and input.
A
compare script
that checks the accuracy of the results against a reference.
A
screening script
that runs the instrumented code multiple times for each kernel, first with decreasing mantissa bits until the comparison fails, and then with the smallest working mantissa size and decreasing exponent bits.
Figure 3. Required mantissa and exponent bit counts for an instrumented reduction kernel measured with a Verificarlo-based implementation of the described analysis workflow
Once this setup is in place, re-run the screening after each code change to track precision requirements. Measured precision requirements for different implementations of a reduction kernel vary (Figure 3).
The results depend on the input and comparison threshold. Here, all kernels would pass a simple FP32 run (Figure 4) without providing an insight into the numerical properties. The baseline is likely to fail with either a slightly larger input or a stricter comparison. The algorithm choice may also come with additional constraints.
Figure 4. Memory layout of typical floating point formats
The code instrumentation can be performed at three levels:
The
library level:
Some libraries offer configurable precision, though only to a limited extent. The emulated matrix multiplications in
cuBLAS
, for example, allow screening the precision requirements of GEMMs by explicitly setting the mantissa bit count.
The
language level:
The native floating-point types can be replaced with a generic one.
NVIDIA CCCL
provides such a type, with both compile-time and runtime configuration of mantissa and exponent bits.
The
compiler level:
A completely non-intrusive and mostly automatic instrumentation can be achieved by replacing floating-point operations with a software implementation during compilation. The
Verificarlo project
takes this approach with its VPREC backend, but is limited to CPU code.
A complete instrumentation also covers dependencies and standard math functions. The instrumented code will be much slower, but the runs can be largely parallelized across HPC resources.
To move from analysis to implementation, start by adding FP64↔FP32 conversion infrastructure around your application’s hot path or a subset of it. Then create type-configurable versions of the functions and kernels in that region. For an initial implementation, keep everything exceeding FP32 requirements as an FP64 island; each subsequent iteration can reduce the FP64 footprint further.
Following this workflow, the original analysis of the Davidson algorithm, based on Verificarlo, indicated that large parts of the code could run with FP32 arithmetic and storage. The FFTs, the application of the Hamiltonian, and the orbital updates run in FP32, while the subspace eigenproblem, the tall-skinny GEMMs behind the subspace matrices, as well as the energies and convergence measures remain in FP64.
The tall-skinny GEMMs in the Rayleigh-Ritz projection were the remaining FP64 bottleneck. Pure FP32 accumulation here is insufficient as the output feeds directly into a numerically sensitive eigenvalue solver. The split-k algorithm resolves this by breaking the dot products into FP32 chunks with a final FP64 accumulation step (Figure 5).
Figure 5. a) Naive tall-skinny GEMM, scalar products cause long sums in FP32, requires FP64 to reach accuracy target b) Mixed precision algorithm performing small FP32 GEMMs with a final FP64 accumulation step, all matrices kept in FP32 storage
Results
In VASP, convergence is controlled by the EDIFF parameter, which specifies the threshold for the total energy change between electronic iterations within an ionic step. Below that threshold, convergence is reached.
The default is 10
-4
eV, while some calculations go down to 10
-6
eV or lower. For reference, FP32 provides around 7 significant decimal digits of precision. EDIFF is an absolute threshold that varies by system and typically scales with atom count, so there is no single best setting.
The mixed-precision Davidson implementation converges to an EDIFF of 10
-4
to 10
-6
eV depending on the input; continuing with FP64 allows the calculation to converge below the FP32 noise floor.  On GaAsBi-64, FP32 enables a 2× speed-up at EDIFF = 10
-5
eV, and the combined FP32→FP64 run is 1.5× faster than pure FP64 at EDIFF = 10⁻⁸ eV (Figure 6).
Figure 6. Convergence trajectory comparison for GaAsBi64 on RTX PRO 6000
On H100 and H200, where FP64 Tensor Cores match FP32 throughput, mixed precision delivers only marginal end-to-end gains. The benefit is concentrated in hardware with a high FP32:FP64 ratio such as the RTX PRO 6000, where the FP32 Davidson solver runs 3x–7x faster, delivering roughly 2x end-to-end acceleration (Figure 7).
Figure 7. Projected speed-ups of complete VASP runs with Daviator in FP32 vs. FP64 across different GPU targets. The speed-ups are a weighted average of 13 representative inputs from the OMat24 dataset
Enabling mixed precision
Daviator’s mixed precision can be enabled by setting LDAVIATOR_MIXED_PRECISION to 1 (0 is FP64). Within an ionic step, the calculation starts in mixed precision (with FP32 storage) until a configurable threshold DAVIATOR_EDIFF_FP32 or a number of SCF steps DAVIATOR_SWITCH_TO_FP64_AFTER_STEP is reached. For most inputs LAVIATOR_EDIFF_FP32 works well from 10
-4
to 10
-5
.
The following INCAR parameters are available to configure the use of mixed precision specifically for Daviator (Table 1).
INCAR Parameter
Values
Description
LDAVIATOR_MIXED_PRECISION
False = FP64
True = FP32
Enable/Disable Mixed Precision (FP32 = mixed arithmetic and FP32 storage in Daviator)
DAVIATOR_EDIFF_FP32
real number > 0 in eV
EDIFF threshold for FP32
DAVIATOR_SWITCH_TO_FP64_AFTER_STEP
Integer N >= 0, switch to FP64 after electronic step N (N=0 is FP64)
-1 = FP32 only, i.e. converge to DAVIATOR_EDIFF_FP32, then stop
-2 = dynamic. i.e. switch to FP64 after DAVIATOR_EDIFF_FP32 convergence
Selects when an ionic step switches from reduced precision to FP64.
Table 1. INCAR parameters for enabling and configuring mixed precision in Daviator
The INCAR for a run that uses FP32 until EDIFF = 5
-5
eV and then switches to FP64 until EDIFF = 5
-7
eV would look like this:
ALGO = Normal
EDIFF = 5e-07
[...]
LDAVIATOR = True
LDAVIATOR_MIXED_PRECISION = True
DAVIATOR_SWITCH_TO_FP64_AFTER_STEP = -2
DAVIATOR_EDIFF_FP32 = 5e-05
Hardware requirements and availability
A VASP user license is required. Daviator and its mixed precision option will be available on any NVIDIA GPU through the NVIDIA ALCHEMI VASP microservice; add the INCAR parameters above to activate it.
What both layers deliver at scale
The
Open Materials 2024 (OMat24) inorganic materials dataset
contains over 100 million VASP data points (total energy, forces, and stress) from molecular dynamics (“AIMD”)​, relaxation (“rattled-relax”),​ and static (“rattled”)​ calculations for MLIP training and validation.
To estimate the time and cost to compute this dataset, we extrapolated from a benchmarked sample of 13 representative inputs across the dataset’s system-size distribution. The individual benchmark runs were tuned to maximize resource utilisation and overall throughput, assuming multiple parallel runs per node. While OMat24 was generated with real-space projectors, the benchmarks and projections here use the more precise reciprocal-space projector setting in VASP (INCAR: LREAL=False).
On the same number of cloud instances, VASP + Daviator is up to 22x faster than VASP on CPU nodes, and up to 7x faster than VASP without Daviator on GPU (Figure 8). For a batch of eight small systems on one GPU, the NVIDIA ALCHEMI VASP microservice raises throughput a further 3–5x.
Figure 8. Projected runtime in million instance hours of cloud resources for the OMat24 dataset using different hardware targets and VASP with/without Daviator in FP64 and FP32
To estimate the price of the data set generation, we applied a geometric mean of the on-demand prices of AWS, Azure, CoreWeave and Google. On datacenter GPUs, the existing OpenACC GPU support in VASP is more expensive than the corresponding CPU computation.
However, the combination with Daviator reduces the cost to roughly 35% of the CPU cost on H100/200 and B200, with mixed precision contributing up to $200,000 in additional savings. The overall lowest price-point—around 25% of the CPU cost—is achieved on RTX PRO 6000 using VASP with Daviator and FP32 (Figure 9).
Figure 9. Projected cloud cost in $, millions USD for the OMat24 dataset
What’s next for GPU-native DFT
For standard DFT, GPUs are now the clear choice for VASP. For teams building MLIP training pipelines at the scale of OMat24 and beyond, VASP + Daviator delivers a GPU-native workflow end-to-end with cost savings of 60–75% over CPU, or approximately $5–6M USD for a dataset the size of OMat24.

items.title: Accelerating development for massive Git repositories Meet Another Build File Service (ABFS), Google's open-source content-addressable filesystem and build cache that cuts Android
items.content:
Accelerating development for massive Git repositories
- Google Developers Blog
Accelerating development for massive Git repositories
NOV. 17, 2026
The Android ABFS Team
Share
Facebook
Twitter
LinkedIn
Mail
Android’s source code is big – the Android 17 open source release has
1,084
Git
repositories,
1.62 million
files, and takes
300 GB
for a built workspace. Additionally, in a typical Android source tree with hardware vendor code and first-party applications, the size increases by
2-3x
.
Traditionally, it took over 30 minutes to fetch Android Open Source Project (AOSP) source code and well over an hour to build on even highly capable developer workstations. As software development evolved over the last 2 years, modern coding harnesses and LLMs have accelerated the development of many projects. These tools are used today for Android operating system development, but the long sync and build times make them less efficient. Both human developers and agents need quick setup, parallel workspaces, and fast build-and-test iteration times.
We built Another Build File Service (ABFS) to address these bottlenecks. ABFS is a full suite of software across a Linux kernel filesystem module, user-space daemons, and server-side infrastructure. ABFS uses content-addressability across the entire stack to lazy-load and cache source code, developer workspaces, intermediate build files, and build results.
Today, we are excited to announce that
ABFS is open source on GitHub
.
The impact of ABFS to Android is:
Reduced checkout times from ~36 minutes to
under 8 seconds
.
Reduced full build times from ~80 minutes to
just over 2 minutes
.
Enabled parallel agentic workflows across multiple workspaces and agent orchestrators.
Shared cache reuses up to
100%
of build actions across continuous integration (CI) and developer workspaces.
ABFS already powers parallel workflows for developers and agents in Android, but it is designed to scale to other massive Git-based projects.
Case Study: Android
In the Android build system, developers define build rules in Blueprint files (
Android.bp
), Soong compiles them into Ninja files, and
Ninja
executes the final build graph (see the
Android build overview
). Similar to the
Make build tool
, Ninja is
timestamp-based
. If a build step’s input file is newer than the existing output file, Ninja rebuilds the output file.
Code Size
Analyzing the
AOSP code
for Android 17 shows the sheer disk footprint and file count involved in a single checkout and build.
Table of Android Open Source Project (AOSP) scale for Android 17: 1,084 Git projects, 1,620,371 regular files, 324,457 directories, 161 GB total code size, and 155 GB build output.
In a typical Android tree that includes hardware-specific repositories, board support packages, first-party applications, form-factor-specific code, etc., the code size is 2–3 times the size of AOSP
(over 3,000 Git repositories),
compounded across multiple active SKU and legacy maintenance branches.
Build Cacheability
Building the Cuttlefish emulator target executes a build graph with
192,249
Ninja actions. While local incremental builds are fast once a tree is already built, every new workspace, branch switch, or ephemeral agent session starts cold.
Even though typical developer changes touch only 1-10 different Git projects, someone building locally without any remote execution might waste up to
80 minutes on a 64-core
machine repeating work their CI system already built. Even if a developer edits a core library like
system/libbase
,
97%
of the build graph is identical to the CI build.
Unspecified Dependencies
Sharing cached build outputs across CI and local machines is also tricky in a codebase of Android's age and rate of change. Build rules occasionally introduce
hidden dependencies
(such as passing an undeclared schema file inside raw compiler flags),
over-declared inputs
, or
undeclared outputs
. In timestamp-based builds, hidden dependencies silently produce stale incremental artifacts, forcing developers to wipe output directories and run clean builds.
Solution: ABFS
ABFS makes building Android fast by replacing massive local source checkouts with a virtual, content-addressable filesystem (CASFS). ABFS streams files on demand only when a build actually touches them and utilizes shared build caching to help eliminate redundant downloads and compilation.
Architecture diagram showing client-side components (Ninja-go, Tap, Mount Daemon, Cacheman, Local Cache, and the CASFS Kernel Module) and server-side components (ABFS CAS Server and Git-pushers connected to a Git source of truth).
On the server side,
Git-pushers
continuously ingest new Git objects from Gerrit or other Git hosts into a horizontally scalable gRPC
ABFS Content-Addressable Storage (CAS) Server
that indexes Git content, workspace snapshots, and build step results. On the developer host, a local Least Recently Used (LRU)
Cacheman
daemon,
Mount Daemon
, and
Tap
utility connect user-space build tools to the kernel filesystem so checkouts and builds stream only what they need. See the
full ABFS architecture on GitHub
.
Filesystem
At the core of the client is a virtual filesystem called
Content-Addressable Storage Filesystem (CASFS)
, a Linux kernel module that exposes Git SHA content hashes via extended attributes. When a file's hash is set, CASFS populates its metadata immediately and downloads file bytes via Cacheman only when needed:
$ touch hello
$ abfs hash --set cc628ccd10742baea8241c5924df992b5c019f71 hello   # metadata only
$ ls -l hello      # name and size are available; content is not downloaded yet
-rw-r----- 1 user primarygroup 6 Nov  3 00:11 hello
$ cat hello        # content is lazy-loaded on first read
world
Shell
Copied
Initial checkouts download only lightweight directory metadata prepopulated with Git hashes. CASFS uses Git's object model natively, allowing standard
git
and
repo
operations to work transparently.
Correct two-phase build caching
CASFS can also
tap
build processes.
Tapping
records every file actually read, written, or deleted into lists called
patches
, which are stored alongside cached build outputs.
Ninja-go
replaces timestamp checks with two-phase content-addressable caching:
Phase 1 - Declared key lookup:
Ninja-go hashes a step’s command, environment, and declared input hashes to fetch candidate results from prior CI or developer builds.
Phase 2 - Read-patch verification:
Before accepting and applying a candidate result, ABFS verifies the candidate’s recorded read patch against the current CASFS state. In the common case, this read patch will match the filesystem state and then the write patch is applied.
If even a hidden dependency has a different hash on disk, ABFS rejects the stale candidate and reruns the step with tapping enabled. This preserves clean-build correctness even when the build graph is incomplete.
Ninja-go accelerates Ninja-based builds like Android and Chrome; other build systems can integrate with ABFS's caching APIs using the same model (see the
two-phase caching walkthrough on GitHub
).
Synchronized workspaces
Each mounted checkout attaches to a persistent
workspace
that eagerly syncs modified files,
git
state, and
repo
state through Cacheman to the ABFS CAS Server—keeping mounts synchronized across sessions or across multiple developer hosts.
Sorry, your browser doesn't support playback for this video
Results
The benchmarks below show the mean time of 3 Android runs on a GCE
n2d-standard-64
VM with 64 vCPUs and 256 GB of RAM. The ABFS remote server was running in the same cloud network as the client.
Source checkout
Note: The “Current” flow used repo init --partial-clone and repo sync -j8 as documented in official Android documentation (higher -j values hit Gerrit rate-limiting on android.googlesource.com).
Sorry, your browser doesn't support playback for this video
Build
Note: All of these builds used lunch aosp_cf_x86_64_only_phone-aosp_current-userdebug and m droid to build.
Sorry, your browser doesn't support playback for this video
Checkout and build demo
Link to Youtube Video
(visible only when JS is disabled)
Unlocking agent development
Because ABFS does lazy loading and local cache deduplication, developers and their agents can now mount multiple concurrent Android workspaces on a single machine, benefit from a shared local build cache, and achieve massive scale in development time.
# Mount 5 distinct Android release branches side-by-side in under 8 seconds each
$ abfs mount -b android-latest-release   /ws/a17
$ abfs mount -b android16-qpr2-release   /ws/a16qpr2
$ abfs mount -b android16-release        /ws/a16
$ abfs mount -b android15-release        /ws/a15
$ abfs mount -b android14-release        /ws/a14
Shell
Copied
An agent can check out a full Android tree in
under 10 seconds
and perform a full build
in under 10 minutes
. Agent swarms are empowered to iterate, review, and test in parallel, which can lead to higher quality solutions and speed.
In the demo below, an agent makes a
system/libbase
fix on the latest AOSP release, then 4 parallel agents simultaneously backport, build, and test the fix across 4 more AOSP releases on a single VM.
Sorry, your browser doesn't support playback for this video
Agent development demo
Link to Youtube Video
(visible only when JS is disabled)
Note: AOSP releases before Android 17 require some patching to work with ABFS.
Extending beyond Google and Android
We released
ABFS as open source
because we want developers, Android partners, and any large-scale Git-based project to benefit from what we have learned and be able to scale.
While Android’s Soong/Ninja pipeline was the first acceleration target, ABFS was built to be extensible to other build systems. Content-addressable build systems like Bazel map naturally onto CASFS and there is already a
proof-of-concept integration with Bazel
. Chromium, the Android Common Kernel, and other Google projects are exploring ABFS compatibility.
Explore
ABFS
,
CASFS
, and
Ninja-go
on GitHub, and reach out to us at abfs@google.com.
For help with the Google Cloud server-side, infrastructure-as-code, and CASFS for Cloud Workstations and Kubernetes, please reach out to abfs-gcp@google.com.
Acknowledgements
We’d like to extend a special thanks to our significant contributors for their work on this project:
Haamed Gheibi, Erik Sanders, Rob Seymour, Taylor Santiago, Andrew Hsieh, Eric Taseski, Kiyoung Kim, Hung-Wei Chen, Jose “Pepe” Galmes, Ronald Li, Yu-Che Wang, Roger Ellis, Sandeep Patil, Amith Dsouza and the entire Android Build team

items.content:
Build full-stack Android apps with Gemini in Google AI Studio
- Google Developers Blog
Build full-stack Android apps with Gemini in Google AI Studio
NOV. 17, 2026
Mike Taylor-Cai
Product Manager
Google AI Studio
Share
Facebook
Twitter
LinkedIn
Mail
Google AI Studio, with Gemini 4 Carbon and Hydrogen, now enables you to build and ship full-stack, Android applications and publish to the Play Store in minutes. You can now go from a single prompt to a production-ready Kotlin Android app complete with data persistence, user sign-in, and AI features. Simply bring your idea and the Google AI Studio Build agent takes care of the entire setup. From configuring your database to securely calling the
Gemini API
, you can rapidly build and test on your own device directly from the Play Store at no cost.
Alongside full-stack Firebase backend provisioning, a major wave of upgrades is rolling out across the Android development workflow in
Google AI Studio
. Developers can now iterate in a faster, high-definition (HD) Android emulator with real-time audio output, send one-click emulator screenshots directly to the coding agent for visual UI changes, and style apps with custom fonts.
Sorry, your browser doesn't support playback for this video
What’s new at a glance
Here is what is launching today for Android app development in Google AI Studio:
Full-stack persistence and sign-in:
Automatically provision a Cloud Firestore database with Security Rules and Google Sign-In so user data syncs across sessions and devices.
Secure Gemini API calls:
Call Gemini models from your Android app without exposing API keys in your APK, protected by Firebase AI Logic and
Firebase App Check
.
Personal Google Play publishing:
Ship Android apps directly to your personal Google Play library with a standard Google account and install them on your phone in clicks.
Faster, high-definition emulator with audio:
Spin up Android emulators with lower latency, toggle HD video streaming, and test real-time audio output directly in your browser.
One-click screenshot to agent:
Capture a live frame from the running emulator with a single click and attach it to your prompt to guide visual UI edits.
Custom fonts and Android CLI integration:
Style Jetpack Compose UIs with custom typography, backed under the hood by the official Android CLI for reliable project scaffolding and builds.
Go full-stack in minutes with Cloud Firestore, Authentication, and Firebase AI Logic
Previously, Android apps generated in AI Studio were limited to local session storage. Now, when your prompt describes an Android app that needs persistent storage, user sign-in, or generative AI features, the Google AI Studio Build agent proactively detects those requirements. With your confirmation, the agent provisions the backend and wires up your Kotlin codebase automatically:
Persistent, cross-device data with Cloud Firestore:
The Build agent provisions a
Cloud Firestore
database, configures the Firebase Android SDKs, and generates Firebase Security Rules tailored to your data model. Users can start a session on an Android tablet and pick up right where they left off on their phone, with offline caching that syncs automatically when connectivity returns.
Identity management with Firebase Authentication:
When your app needs user profiles or private workspaces, the agent configures
Firebase Authentication
with Google Sign-In and pairs it with per-user authorization rules so users can only read and write their own documents.
Server-side credential protection with Firebase AI Logic:
Hardcoding API keys inside a client APK risks credential extraction. When your Android app calls Gemini models, the Build agent automatically configures
Firebase AI Logic
and enforces
Firebase App Check
using Google Fraud Defense (formerly reCAPTCHA Enterprise). Credentials stay protected server-side, and App Check verifies that incoming requests originate from your authentic, untampered app—both in the browser emulator and on Google Play.
Under the hood, the Build agent automatically adds the Firebase Bill of Materials (BoM) and generates clean, idiomatic Kotlin code for your data and AI layers:
// Generated by Google AI Studio Build agent using Firebase AI Logic & Cloud Firestore
class WorkoutRepository(context: Context) {
private val generativeModel by lazy {
Firebase.ai(backend = GenerativeBackend.googleAI())
.generativeModel("gemini-4-hydrogen")
}
private val db = FirebaseFirestore.getInstance(        context.applicationContext.getString(R.string.firestore_database_id))
suspend fun generateAndSaveWorkout(goal: String, uid: String) {
val response = generativeModel.generateContent("Create a 20-minute workout for: $goal")
val workout = hashMapOf(
"ownerId" to uid,
"goal" to goal,
"plan" to (response.text ?: ""),
"createdAt" to FieldValue.serverTimestamp()
)
db.collection("workouts").add(workout).await()
}
}

Iterate faster with an HD, audio-enabled emulator and visual debugging
Building great mobile interfaces requires a tight visual and interactive feedback loop. Both the in-browser Android emulator and the Build agent's toolchain include new capabilities to help you inspect, hear, and refine your app in real time:
Faster startup and 1200p HD streaming:
Emulators now boot with significantly lower latency so you can test code changes rapidly. Use the
HD toggle
in the emulator toolbar to switch the stream to 1200p high definition, making it easy to inspect fine Jetpack Compose spacing, animations, and dense layouts.
Real-time audio output:
Hear live audio from the Android emulator directly in your browser. You can build and test voice-driven Gemini Live API companions, text-to-speech (TTS) coaches, sound-enabled games, and media apps without leaving Google AI Studio.
One-click screenshot to agent:
Describing a visual layout issue in text can take paragraphs. Click
Take a screenshot
in the emulator toolbar to capture the live app screen and attach it directly to your prompt. Point out the adjustment you want—such as tightening card padding, fixing contrast, or realigning a toolbar—and Gemini updates the Kotlin UI code with full visual context.
Custom fonts support:
Give your app a distinct visual identity by asking the agent for custom fonts. The Build agent automatically downloads, configures, and applies your chosen typography across your Compose theme.
Powered by the Android CLI under the hood:
Behind the scenes, the Google AI Studio Build agent now uses the official
Android CLI
to scaffold project structures, query current Android documentation, and execute Gradle builds, reducing build errors and supporting more complex multi-screen architectures.
Sorry, your browser doesn't support playback for this video
Ship straight to your phone with Google Play
Testing in an emulator accelerates iteration, but nothing replaces running your app on a physical device. Historically, installing a newly built Android app onto a phone required enabling USB debugging cables, managing signing keystores locally, or setting up a full developer console account.
With
Google Play
integrated directly into Google AI Studio, you can set up a Play account in a few clicks from the publish panel and publish your app straight to your personal Google Play library. Google AI Studio builds and signs the Android App Bundle (.aab) behind the scenes, so you can immediately download and run your custom Android app on your phone directly from Google Play.
What’s next: Start building your Android app today
All of these features are rolling out in Google AI Studio today. To get started, open
Google AI Studio Build
, select the
Android
chip at the top of the workspace, and try one of these prompts:
"Build an Android workout coach app that uses the Gemini API to generate personalized daily routines, reads cues aloud with audio, and saves workout history across devices using Cloud Firestore and Google Sign-In."
"Create a collaborative family recipe Android app with custom serif typography where users sign in with Google, snap photos of ingredients to generate recipe ideas with Gemini, and sync shared grocery lists in Firestore."
Explore the
Google AI Studio documentation
and
Firebase Android documentation
to learn more, try building your own full-stack Android app at
aistudio.google.com/apps
, and share what you build on X with
@GoogleDevs
,
@GoogleAIStudio
, and
@AndroidDev
.

items.title: Gemini 4 Hydrogen: a faster model for general purpose robotics Google's Gemini 4 Hydrogen brings strong spatial and embodied reasoning capabilities to a fast, efficient model built
items.content:
Gemini 4 Hydrogen: a faster model for general purpose robotics
- Google Developers Blog
Gemini 4 Hydrogen: a faster model for general purpose robotics
NOV. 17, 2026
Alex Gruenstein
Distinguished Software Engineer
Gabe Cohen
Senior Director, PM, Robotics
Gemini Robotics Team
Share
Facebook
Twitter
LinkedIn
Mail
Over the past month,
Gemini 4 Argon
and
Gemini 4 Carbon
brought
frontier physical reasoning to robotics
: understanding 3D scenes, reconstructing real environments in simulation, practicing tasks in sim before running them on hardware, and directly controlling robot arms from camera images. Last week, we introduced
Gemini 4 Hydrogen
, which brings strong spatial and embodied reasoning to a much faster model built for speed and efficiency.
To help developers put Hydrogen to work, today we're launching the
Robotics plugin on
Google Antigravity
: a set of skills for hardware onboarding, simulation and robot control turning Antigravity into a one-stop robotics workbench. Together, they enable a developer to go from a robot in a box to one that can perform a working application in an afternoon. To install the plugin, open Antigravity, go to
Customizations
and search for Robotics on the
Build With Google
shelf.
Hydrogen for agentic robotic control
Gemini 4 Argon and Carbon showed that a general model can drive a robot arm directly, and Gemini 4 Hydrogen preserves that ability. Give it a goal in plain language and a camera view, and it plans the task, writes and runs the control code, and keeps adjusting until the job is done. On the
Artificial Analysis Robotics 0.1 benchmark
, Gemini 4 Hydrogen controls a real 6-axis arm through eight everyday tabletop tasks, from pouring a drink to packing blocks into a box.
Hydrogen scores 58
, similar to Argon at a lower cost per token.
Embodied reasoning in a fast generalist
Hydrogen brings the specialized skills of our Gemini Robotics ER 2 (Embodied Reasoning) models into the core Gemini 4 model series, and it beats them on nearly every axis. On the public
ERQA
benchmark
, Hydrogen outperforms Gemini Robotics ER 2 on spatial reasoning tasks such as multi-view correspondence and 3D trajectory reasoning.
For developers using
Gemini Robotics ER 2
today, we recommend trying out Gemini 4 Hydrogen for these workloads.
Antigravity becomes a robotics workbench
A fast, capable model is only half the story. Building a robot application has always meant gluing together drivers, calibration scripts, simulators, perception code, and a UI, which requires robotics expertise and a lot of time. The new
Robotics plugin
for Google Antigravity packages that work into skills Gemini can use on your behalf:
Robot bring-up:
Installs drivers, discovers cameras, calibrates the arm, and verifies safe motion, starting from a USB cable.
MuJoCo in Antigravity:
Builds and previews simulated scenes and assets inside Antigravity, so you can try ideas in sim before touching hardware.
Perception and control:
Uses Gemini’s spatial understanding to find objects, plan grasps, and control the robot in a closed loop.
Application building:
Leverages Gemini’s coding skills to generate the controller, simulation, and complete a full Real-to-Sim-to-Real application development in a seamless, one-stop shop environment.
Sorry, your browser doesn't support playback for this video
With the Antigravity Robotics plugin, it just takes one prompt to start rendering a MuJoCo scene
Here's what that looks like end to end: set up a robot and build real applications.
1. Set up: from USB connection to a moving robot in minutes
Starting from an empty desk, a developer plugs an
I2RT YAM arm
and an external depth camera into a laptop and asks Hydrogen in Antigravity to bring it up. The plugin's Skills install the software, find the camera, calibrate the arm, and run test motions.
The arm is calibrated and ready for tasks in about 10 minutes.
A similar flow also brings up a low-cost
SO-ARM101
arm and an industrial grade
FR3
Duo from scratch to live waving.
Sorry, your browser doesn't support playback for this video
YAM onboarding (~10 min elapsed). From the USB connection to a calibrated arm ready for tasks.
Once the robot is live, you can use a simple prompt to create a basic task within just a few minutes:
Use the arm to make some fun dance moves
Pick up a pen on the table
Stack snacks on top of each other
2. Create high quality simulation assets and “vibe sim”
Once the robot is live, the next step is building a simulation you can trust. With the Robotics plugin, MuJoCo runs directly inside Antigravity with dedicated creation, auditing, and rendering skills. This allows you to build and preview high-quality simulated scenes and assets—whether described, imported from links/documents, or uploaded via workspace photos—right alongside your code. You can then "vibe sim" by adjusting shapes, positions, and physical properties through chat to verify reaching and grasping before deploying to physical hardware.
Sorry, your browser doesn't support playback for this video
Create an asset with just one prompt referencing a product information page.
3. Build an application
The workbench with Hydrogen and Robotics plugins lets you go from an idea to a repeatable working application in real world in a much shorter time, by iterating and validating it in simulation.
Snack-sorting conveyor: from whiteboard idea to a working sorter in an hour
A developer starts with a whiteboard sketch: a conveyor belt carrying mixed snacks, with a robot arm picking and sorting them into bins. From one prompt of the task with images of a real scene, Hydrogen constructs an interactive MuJoCo simulation of the cell, testing and validating the grasping policy in sim across multiple runs. The developer then deploys the verified policy directly to the robot in the real world. When nuances emerge (such as tuning gripper closure force or refining sorting rules), the developer iterates in natural language, asking Hydrogen to adjust the controller to iterate. Within about an hour end-to-end, the arm reliably sorts snacks off the moving belt.
Sorry, your browser doesn't support playback for this video
Conveyor snack sorting, real-to-sim-to-real. From a whiteboard brainstorm through a MuJoCo simulation to sorting on a live conveyor.
Soap store: a storefront that fulfills its own orders
Hydrogen's efficiency makes it practical to run a multi-step robot application all day. In this example, a developer uses Hydrogen to build a small web storefront for a soap shop, then connects it to two YAM Pro arms. When an order comes in, the arms set out a packing bin, pick the ordered mint and citrus bars, and pull a printed thank-you note from a printer.
Sorry, your browser doesn't support playback for this video
Soap Store (1× dev / 5× fulfillment). From building the storefront with Hydrogen to dual-arm order packing.
Chess playing robot
With just a few prompts, the FR3 Duo simulates a chess board and then can play chess against itself or take on human opponents.
Sorry, your browser doesn't support playback for this video
From idea, to simulation, to playing chess.
Making robotics accessible
Gemini 4 Argon pushes the ceiling of physical reasoning. Gemini 4 Hydrogen makes those capabilities fast and affordable enough to use every day, and the Antigravity Robotics plugin puts them in a workbench where anyone can go from a robot in a box to a working application. We can't wait to see what you build.
You can share your own creations and use cases on the plugin’s GitHub
discussions page
. If you have any ideas, custom skills, or derived work you think would be helpful, please let us know—we’ll keep improving the plugins.
Getting started
Google Antigravity + Robotics plugin:
Select
Gemini 4 Hydrogen
(
gemini-4-hydrogen
) in
Google Antigravity
and install the
Robotics plugin:
go to
Customizations
and search for Robotics on the
Build With Google
shelf. Then try a prompt:
"Bring up my SO-101 arm and make it wave."
Google Antigravity is for paid Google AI Pro or Ultra subscribers.
Gemini API:
Use
gemini-4-hydrogen
in the
Interactions API
, with day-one support in the
google-genai
SDKs.
Google AI Studio
:
Try spatial prompts, live camera streams, and structured tool calls in the browser.

Introducing Perplexity Frontier Research
Our mission and research agenda in advancing autonomous discovery.
Nov 16, 2026
Authors
Perplexity Research
We are excited to launch
Perplexity Frontier Research
, a new initiative to advance the frontier of algorithms, models, and evaluations, in the open.
We aim to build an automatic research scientist, an AI system that can conduct research on its own. Research is a loop that involves asking the right questions, hypothesizing, designing experiments, analyzing results, navigating ambiguity, and updating beliefs. In contrast to black-box predictions in narrowly defined settings, this effort is designed to produce new interpretable knowledge that advances our understanding across a broad range of applications.
This ambition inspires new algorithms, models, and evaluations. We will be particularly considering six pillars: multi-agent orchestration, pre-training, continual learning, reinforcement learning, systems, and evaluations. Within each of these areas, we will explore a variety of foundational questions. For example, can we propose new, more efficient architectures? Can we synthesize data that enables broader generalization? Under what conditions is multi-agent collaboration most effective? Can we create evaluations that measure research ability and extrapolation, rather than only recall?
This is an environment where one has the opportunity to advance the frontier of research, and share results openly. We will release papers, blog posts, data, models, and code. Our research will also be supported by considerable computational resources, in excess of 10,000 GPUs. And our findings shape a product used by millions of curious people, the most challenging test of all.

Cohere Expands Its Sovereign AI Platform with AISLE and cubic
Expanding the sovereign AI platform with new capabilities for cyber defense, secure software development, and mission-critical enterprise workflows
Blog
Written By
Cohere Team
Tags
Company News
Sovereign AI
Share
AI isn’t a shortcut.
It’s how business gets ahead.
Contact sales
Over the past year, we've seen a fundamental shift in how organizations approach AI. Enterprises and governments are deploying AI into the workflows that matter most, from cybersecurity and software development to mission-critical operations and decision-making. As they do, their requirements are becoming increasingly clear: they need AI systems that are powerful, secure, and under their control.
At Cohere, we've long believed organizations shouldn't have to choose between cutting-edge AI and control. They should be able to deploy advanced AI while maintaining ownership of their data, infrastructure, and operations. That's the foundation of sovereign AI.
Today, we're excited to share two important milestones in that journey. We're pleased to announce the completion of our acquisition of AISLE, the company building autonomous systems for vulnerability discovery and remediation. We're also welcoming the team behind cubic, one of the leading AI-powered code review platforms, to Cohere.
Together, these additions strengthen the sovereign AI platform we're building for organizations around the world. With
AISLE
and cubic we’ve completed four strategic M&A transactions this year, following
Aleph Alpha
,
Reliant AI
to expand our capabilities across frontier AI, biopharma and healthcare, cybersecurity, and software development.
Cybersecurity is a defining frontier of AI
As AI becomes embedded in critical systems and workflows, security is becoming a defining requirement for adoption. Organizations increasingly need AI that can operate inside private clouds, on-premises and air-gapped environments while meeting rigorous requirements around privacy, governance, and compliance.
That's why we're excited to officially welcome AISLE to Cohere. When we announced our intent to acquire AISLE, we outlined a shared belief: the future of AI depends on the ability to secure both AI systems and the software infrastructure that powers them. As organizations deploy AI into increasingly sensitive environments, cyber resilience becomes foundational to trust.
AISLE’s co-founders are taking leadership roles spanning cybersecurity, corporate security, AI security research and frontier model development. Ondrej Vlcek will become Senior Vice President, Cohere Cyber, and lead the newly established cybersecurity business. Jaya Baloo will become Cohere’s Chief Information Security Officer, overseeing security across the company. Stanislav Fort will become Vice President, AI Security, joining Cohere’s core model research and training efforts while leading AI security research.
Cohere also plans to make a substantial long-term investment in Prague, expanding AISLE’s existing presence and establishing the city as its global center for AI cybersecurity and autonomous security systems.
AISLE brings world-class expertise in autonomous security research and vulnerability discovery.
Their work has demonstrated how specialized AI systems can identify, validate, and remediate vulnerabilities at a speed and scale that helps defenders stay ahead of an increasingly complex threat landscape.
Today, that expertise has become the foundation of Cohere Cyber, our cybersecurity business focused on helping enterprises, governments, and critical infrastructure operators build and operate secure, cyber-resilient AI systems. Together, we're building cyber defense capabilities that help organizations deploy AI with confidence in even the most demanding environments.
Bringing secure coding to enterprise scale
Software development is one of the most widely adopted enterprise applications of AI. But organizations need more than systems that generate code. They need AI that can understand complex codebases, review changes, identify vulnerabilities, maintain software quality, and operate within strict security boundaries. That's what attracted us to cubic.
The team has built an industry-leading AI-powered code review platform that helps engineering organizations review code, find bugs and vulnerabilities, understand complex codebases, and automatically remediate issues. Their review agents have consistently ranked among the strongest performers on code review benchmarks and were built for the environments many enterprise customers operate in, including on-premises and air-gapped deployments.
Led by founder and CEO Paul Sanglé-Ferrière, the team brings expertise across AI, security, developer tools, distributed systems, and enterprise software. They will establish Cohere's secure coding vertical, helping accelerate the integration of enterprise-grade coding capabilities into our platform while meeting the security, governance, and deployment requirements our customers demand. Their work strengthens our ability to help organizations build, maintain, and secure software using AI within their own environments and under their own control.
Building AI for the world's most critical industries
What connects AISLE and cubic is more than technical excellence. Both teams have built products for organizations operating in environments where security, reliability, governance, and control are non-negotiable.
Their work reflects a broader shift we're seeing across the market. Organizations increasingly want AI they can deploy on their own terms. They want systems that fit within their security requirements, regulatory obligations, and operational realities without becoming dependent on systems they can't inspect, adapt, or control.
We believe this is where the next phase of AI adoption will be won. By bringing together frontier models, secure deployment infrastructure, cyber defense, and purpose-built applications, we're continuing to build a sovereign AI platform that gives organizations more capability, more security, and more control.
Looking ahead
The future of AI won't be defined by models alone. It will be defined by the systems, workflows, and infrastructure built around them. The question is whether organizations can deploy AI securely and at scale across the systems that matter most. That's the promise of sovereign AI.
Welcoming AISLE and cubic to Cohere strengthens our ability to deliver on that vision. Together, we're building a sovereign AI platform that enterprises and governments can trust to operate in their most sensitive environments, power their most critical workflows, and realize the full potential of AI while maintaining control of their data, infrastructure, and operations.
We're excited to welcome both teams to Cohere and look forward to what we'll build together.

Microsoft Azure Cobalt 200 VMs reach general availability, bringing Arm-powered performance to cloud and agentic AI workloads  - Arm Newsroom
